title: Enone + R2CuLi → 1,4 (conjugate) addition

steps.label: The cuprate's methyl adds to the β-carbon (1,4-addition), giving an enolate
steps.note: Soft nucleophile, soft (β) carbon. The negative charge ends up shared between the α-carbon and oxygen.

steps.label: Acid workup: the enolate's α-carbon takes a proton, giving the ketone
steps.note: Protonating oxygen first gives the enol, which tautomerizes to this same ketone.

why: Cuprates are soft nucleophiles, so they add to the soft β-carbon (1,4) rather than the C=O carbon. The enolate that forms is protonated on workup and tautomerizes back to the ketone, now carrying a methyl at the β-position.

traps.explains: That's 1,2-addition, which is what a hard nucleophile like CH3MgBr or CH3Li does. Cuprates add 1,4.
The methyl lands on the β-carbon (two carbons from C=O), not the α-carbon next to it.
Cuprates don't reduce the C=O. After workup the ketone is still there.

review: Arrows show the simplified 'carbanion adds to β-carbon' picture, not the Cu(III) oxidative-addition mechanism. Check this is acceptable as the drilled key step (it is the standard textbook simplification).

title: Enone + CH3MgBr → 1,2-addition (allylic alcohol)

steps.label: The Grignard's methyl adds to the carbonyl carbon (1,2-addition), giving an alkoxide
steps.note: Hard nucleophile, hard electrophile: the C=O carbon, not the β-carbon.

steps.label: Acid workup: the alkoxide takes a proton
steps.note: The C=C is untouched: a tertiary allylic alcohol.

why: A Grignard is a hard, highly reactive nucleophile, so it attacks the hard, most positive carbon: the C=O carbon (1,2-addition), not the β-carbon. Workup protonates the alkoxide to a tertiary allylic alcohol; the C=C is untouched. Compare (CH3)2CuLi, which adds 1,4.

traps.explains: That's 1,4 (conjugate) addition, which is what a soft cuprate like (CH3)2CuLi does. Grignards add 1,2 to the C=O.
The Grignard adds once, to the C=O. Nothing reduces the C=C, so the product is still an alkene.
Mild aqueous acid workup only protonates the alkoxide. Dehydrating the alcohol to a diene would need heat and strong acid.

distractors.explains: A cuprate adds 1,4, so this gives 3-methylcyclohexanone, a ketone with no OH.
An alcohol's O–H just protonates the Grignard (giving methane). There is no C=O for the methyl to add to.

title: Enone + n-BuLi → 1,2-addition (allylic alcohol)

steps.label: The butyl group adds to the carbonyl carbon (1,2-addition), giving an alkoxide
steps.note: Organolithiums are hard nucleophiles, like Grignards, so they add 1,2.

steps.label: Acid workup: the alkoxide takes a proton

why: Organolithiums, like Grignards, are hard carbon nucleophiles, so they add directly to the C=O carbon (1,2) of an enone. Workup gives a tertiary allylic alcohol with the C=C still in place.

traps.explains: That's 1,4-addition, the cuprate result. To put the butyl on the β-carbon you would use (CH3CH2CH2CH2)2CuLi.
Only the C=O reacts. The organolithium does not reduce the C=C, so the alkene is still there.
BuLi delivers a carbon, not a hydride, so a new C–C bond forms at the carbonyl carbon.

distractors.explains: A cuprate adds 1,4, giving 3-butylcyclopentanone, not an allylic alcohol.
Cyclopentanone has no C=C, so this gives 1-butylcyclopentanol; the target still has the ring alkene.

title: Acid chloride + R2CuLi → ketone (stops there)

steps.label: The cuprate's methyl adds to the acid chloride's carbonyl carbon, giving a tetrahedral intermediate
The C=O re-forms and chloride leaves, giving the ketone
steps.note: Pattern B: addition then elimination. The cuprate is too weak to add to the ketone, so it stops here.

why: Gilman reagents (made from 2 CH3Li + CuI) are soft and much less reactive than Grignards: they substitute the Cl of a reactive acid chloride (pattern B) but do not attack the ketone that forms, so the reaction stops at the ketone. CH3MgBr would add a second time and give a tertiary alcohol.

traps.explains: That's the Grignard result: CH3MgBr adds twice (substitution, then addition to the new ketone). A cuprate is too unreactive to add to a ketone, so it stops after one.
Cuprates don't reduce ketones and workup doesn't either. The product keeps its C=O.
The cuprate replaces the Cl with CH3 before workup, so the acid chloride is gone by the time water is added. No carboxylic acid forms.

distractors.explains: A Grignard adds twice to an acid chloride, so this gives 2-phenyl-2-propanol, not the ketone.
Cuprates are too unreactive to substitute an ester; they need the much more reactive acid chloride.

review: Key-step arrows use the simplified 'carbanion adds to C=O' picture (like u3-gilman-enone), not the Cu(III) oxidative-addition/reductive-elimination mechanism. Also check the methyl benzoate retro distractor: cuprates are generally described as unreactive toward esters. Mechanism: drawn with the same simplified 'methyl anion adds, then Cl⁻ leaves' picture as the key step (no Cu(III) oxidative addition/reductive elimination); there is no acid-workup protonation step since the ketone forms directly.

title: R2CuLi + alkyl halide → coupling (Corey–House)
why: A Gilman reagent (made from 2 CH3Li + CuI) swaps the halogen for one of its R groups, joining two carbon pieces with a new C–C bond. Grignards and organolithiums don't do this cleanly, which is why cuprates are the coupling reagent of choice.

traps.explains: Cuprates are weak bases, so E2 to the alkene is not the main pathway. They couple instead.
That's a Wurtz-type homocoupling of two alkyl halides. The cuprate supplies the CH3 that replaces Br.
The CH3 ends up on the carbon that carried the Br; there is no carbocation and no rearrangement.

distractors.explains: Grignard reagents do not couple cleanly with alkyl halides; you need the cuprate.
Friedel–Crafts alkylation with a 1° chloride rearranges to the 2° carbocation, giving mostly isopropylbenzene (cumene).

review: The Corey–House mechanism is not SN2 (oxidative addition to Cu then reductive elimination); the key step drawn is the simplified 'CH3 replaces Br' arrow pair, which looks like SN2. Check this is acceptable, and that the E2/homocoupling traps are fair.
